cards.subject: The pall, alone, as an illuminated still life, seen straight on at eye level: a small stiff square of white linen standing upright on its edge, propped against a low wooden stand, its face embroidered in gold and deep red thread with a cross between two ears of wheat and a cluster of grapes, a narrow white lace edge on its border. It stands on a ledge of polished black marble that mirrors it; a single warm lamp from the right makes the gold thread glint against the dark. Small, precise, protective. No figures. The card's frame is exactly the attached cards': the coloured initial box at the top-left, one vine-and-flower band to its right along the top and one along the bottom, plain parchment margins down the sides; the deep-blue starred ground and its medallion sit between the two bands and end ABOVE the bottom band.
cards.frame: instead of the arched window, a centred gold-edged QUATREFOIL medallion on a deep blue ground scattered with small gold stars, holding a single object like an illuminated still life; no halo, no figures
cards.basis: The pall is prepared on the credence table with the chalice, corporal and purificator 'if appropriate' (GIRM 118c): it is optional, and the GIRM gives it no form. It covers the chalice; the excerpt is the blessing over the wine the chalice holds, said just before it is placed on the corporal. The traditional pall is a stiffened square of linen, one with the corporal in its origin (the corporal once folded back over the chalice) and in its blessing, 'to cover and wrap the Body and Blood of the Lord' (Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Corporal'); its embroidered cross, wheat and grapes are a traditional choice, not a norm.

cards.subject: The corporal, alone, as an illuminated still life, seen at three-quarters from a little above: a square of fine white linen spread open on the white cloth of the altar, the crisp creases of its folds dividing it into nine small squares, a small cross worked in white thread near its front edge. Nothing stands on it yet. Warm golden dawn light falls from a high window at the left, catching the raised creases and casting long soft shadows across the linen, the altar edge falling away into shadow. Clean, waiting, ready to receive. No figures. The card's frame is exactly the attached cards': the coloured initial box at the top-left, one vine-and-flower band to its right along the top and one along the bottom, plain parchment margins down the sides; the deep-blue starred ground and its medallion sit between the two bands and end ABOVE the bottom band.

cards.basis: The corporal is prepared on the credence table (GIRM 118c) and spread on the altar at the Preparation of the Gifts (GIRM 139), where the paten and chalice are placed on it (the excerpt's rubric; GIRM 151); the altar itself bears 'at least one cloth, white in color' (GIRM 304). The GIRM fixes no material or form: the square of pure white linen, folded in three each way, with at most a small cross, is the traditional corporal (Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Corporal').

The words of the excerpt are that formula. The GIRM gives no form: a white linen oblong folded in three with a small cross is the traditional one, not a prescribed one.

cards.subject: The thurible and its boat, as an illuminated still life, seen from below, looking up: a thurible of gilded brass hangs on its long fine chains from the top of the medallion, its pierced domed lid raised a little on the chains, red coals glowing through the openings, and thick blue-grey smoke curling upward in slow coils. Below it, on a ledge of dark stone, sits the incense boat, a small gilded vessel shaped like a boat with a hinged lid half open, grains of incense showing, and a small spoon laid across it. A shaft of pale sunlight cuts through the smoke in a dim stone apse. Fragrant, rising, solemn. No figures. The card's frame is exactly the attached cards': the coloured initial box at the top-left, one vine-and-flower band to its right along the top and one along the bottom, plain parchment margins down the sides; the deep-blue starred ground and its medallion sit between the two bands and end ABOVE the bottom band.

cards.basis: 'Thurification or incensation is an expression of reverence and of prayer, as is signified in Sacred Scripture (cf. Ps 141 [140]:2; Rev 8:3)' (GIRM 276), the verse of the excerpt. On Sundays and festive days 'a thurible and incense boat, if incense is being used' are prepared (GIRM 119), and the thurifer carries 'a smoking thurible' in the Entrance Procession (GIRM 120a); the priest puts incense into the thurible and blesses it (GIRM 277). The form is not prescribed: a cup on a base with a pierced lid on chains, and a boat for the incense, is the traditional one (Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Censer' and 'Incense').

cards.subject: The aspergillum and its bucket, as an illuminated still life, seen at eye level, a little from the side: a small round bucket of polished silver with a curved handle, full of clear water, and resting in it a silver aspergillum, a slender rod ending in a pierced silver ball, lifted so that bright drops of water fall from the ball back into the bucket. They stand on the pale limestone rim of a baptismal font in fresh, clear spring morning light, the water glittering silver and pale blue. Bright, fresh, cleansing. No figures. The card's frame is exactly the attached cards': the coloured initial box at the top-left, one vine-and-flower band to its right along the top and one along the bottom, plain parchment margins down the sides; the deep-blue starred ground and its medallion sit between the two bands and end ABOVE the bottom band.

The Missal gives the aspergillum no form: the silver bucket and the rod with a pierced ball are the traditional pair, a choice.

The bells shine gold; warm candlelight falls from above and out of view, and the marble squares recede into soft darkness behind them. Bright, expectant, a summons to kneel. No figures. cards.subject: The amice, laid out on a vesting cabinet, as an illuminated still life, seen from steeply above: an oblong of plain white linen spread flat on the dark polished oak top of a sacristy vesting cabinet, a small cross embroidered in white at the middle of its upper edge, its two long white tapes stretched out from the upper corners and trailing over the cabinet's edge. Light through a stained-glass window scatters small patches of blue, gold and ruby across the white linen and the dark wood. Simple, ready, the first vestment. No figures. The card's frame is exactly the attached cards': the coloured initial box at the top-left, one vine-and-flower band to its right along the top and one along the bottom, plain parchment margins down the sides; the deep-blue starred ground and its medallion sit between the two bands and end ABOVE the bottom band.

cards.basis: 'Before the alb is put on, should this not completely cover the ordinary clothing at the neck, an amice should be used' (GIRM 336); all who wear an alb should use a cincture and an amice 'unless, due to the form of the alb, they are not needed' (GIRM 119). The GIRM gives no form: an oblong of white linen with a small cross in the middle and two tapes is the traditional amice, whose vesting prayer calls it galeam salutis, 'the helmet of salvation' (Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Amice'), the words of Eph 6:17 in the excerpt, from the First Reading of Thursday of the Thirtieth Week in Ordinary Time, Year II. White linen: the norms give it no colour.

cards.subject: The alb, hanging, as an illuminated still life, seen straight on and full length: a long white linen alb with narrow sleeves hangs from a plain wooden hanger on a peg against a pale blue-grey plastered wall, its soft vertical folds falling to a deep band of fine white lace that reaches from the knee to the hem, with matching lace at each cuff. Soft morning light from the left models the folds and the lace in pearl and silver-grey shadow. Pure, plain, luminous. No figures. The card's frame is exactly the attached cards': the coloured initial box at the top-left, one vine-and-flower band to its right along the top and one along the bottom, plain parchment margins down the sides; the deep-blue starred ground and its medallion sit between the two bands and end ABOVE the bottom band.

cards.basis: 'The sacred garment common to all ordained and instituted ministers of any rank is the alb, to be tied at the waist with a cincture' (GIRM 336); it is prepared in the sacristy for priest, deacon and other ministers (GIRM 119). White is its name and its traditional colour, a linen tunic to the feet with close sleeves, lace permitted as ornament (Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Alb'); the GIRM leaves the materials to the Conferences (GIRM 343) and wants beauty 'in the material used and in the design' (GIRM 344). The lace border is a traditional choice. The excerpt's Latin is 'amicti sunt stolis albis', clothed in white robes.

Beside it a small clay oil lamp burns with a steady flame; beyond the window, deep blue dusk. The lamplight warms the cord and the stone. Watchful, ready, girded. No figures. cards.subject: The stole, laid over a rail, as an illuminated still life, seen straight on at eye level: a long, narrow stole of violet silk in the Roman manner hangs folded over a polished brass vestment rail, its two ends falling side by side, each end widening into a spade-shaped panel embroidered with a small gold cross above a short gold fringe, a third small gold cross at the middle where it bends over the rail. Behind it a wall of warm grey stone; soft, even afternoon light brings out the sheen of the silk. Humble, penitent, a yoke gladly borne. No figures. The card's frame is exactly the attached cards': the coloured initial box at the top-left, one vine-and-flower band to its right along the top and one along the bottom, plain parchment margins down the sides; the deep-blue starred ground and its medallion sit between the two bands and end ABOVE the bottom band.

cards.basis: 'The stole is worn by the Priest around his neck and hanging down in front of his chest, while it is worn by the Deacon over his left shoulder' (GIRM 340); it is prepared for both with the alb (GIRM 119), the mark of their orders (Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Stole'). It follows the colour of the day (GIRM 346): the card shows violet, the colour of Advent and Lent (346d), because the excerpt is the Lenten Gospel of Saturday of the Second Week of Lent and the violet sets it apart from the white linens of this batch. The crosses at the ends and the middle are traditional; the Church prescribes only the one in the middle (Catholic Encyclopedia). The excerpt's 'best robe' is 'stolam primam' in the Vulgate (content/do Quad2-6).
